title: A Problem in Your Community
prompt:
Write an essay about a problem in your community and how we might solve it. “Community” might refer to your neighborhood, school, grade, city, state, country, age group, race, gender, or any other group you belong to. Your essay can focus on any problems that you see or feel.

Use your personal experience and observations to develop your position, and evidence from your own experience to support your ideas. How do you propose we solve this problem?

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: A Problem in Education
prompt:
Write a critical essay that discusses a problem in education. It might be something you’ve noticed in your own school, in your own classes, or in the way school works more broadly — how students are tested, what gets taught, who gets heard, or anything else you feel strongly about.

Use your personal experience and observations to develop your position, and evidence from your own experience to support your ideas. How do you propose we solve this problem?

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: What Gives You Hope
prompt:
Write an essay about what gives you hope in the world today. When you look around at the world and all of its complexity, and you look ahead to the future, what gives you hope? You might identify problems that you believe you and your generation can solve, changes or innovations that you look forward to, or people and things that inspire your hope in the face of adversity.

Your essay can include how you define hope, what hope looks like for you personally, or the role hope plays in shaping the state of the world today. You might consider the quote, “If despair creates problems, hope can achieve the impossible.” You may use your personal experiences and observations to develop your stance, and evidence from your own life to support your ideas. In some cases, you may use outside sources to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: A Belief You’ve Changed Your Mind About
prompt:
Write an essay about a belief you once held that you no longer hold. What did you used to think — about yourself, about other people, or about the way the world works — and what changed your mind?

Consider what experience, conversation, or piece of evidence made you reconsider, and what it cost you or freed you to let the old belief go. If you’re having trouble choosing, go where the emotional charge is: pick the belief whose change still feels significant to you. Use your personal experience and observations to develop your position, and evidence from your own life to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: A Rule Worth Questioning
prompt:
Write an essay that makes the case for changing a rule, norm, or expectation you think is wrong. It might be a rule at your school, an unwritten expectation in your community, or a norm most people take for granted.

Be specific about what the rule is, who it affects, and why the usual justification for it doesn’t hold up. Then argue for what should replace it. Use your personal experience and observations to develop your position, and evidence from your own experience to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: What We Owe One Another
prompt:
Write an essay about what we owe one another. What responsibilities, if any, do people have to their families, their neighbors, strangers, or future generations — and where do those responsibilities end?

You might ground your argument in a moment when someone showed up for you, or a moment when you had to decide whether to show up for someone else. Use your personal experience and observations to develop your position, and evidence from your own life to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Ambition and Its Costs
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about ambition and what it costs. Drawing on a text we’ve read together, explore what the story suggests about the drive to rise, to win, or to become something more — and what a character gives up in the pursuit.

You might focus on a single character whose ambition drives the story, or compare two characters who want the same thing for different reasons. Consider whether the text treats ambition as a virtue, a danger, or both. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Justice and Loyalty in Conflict
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about what happens when justice and loyalty pull in opposite directions. Using a text we’ve read, examine a moment when a character has to choose between doing what’s right and standing by someone they love.

Consider what the text seems to value more, and whether you agree. You might argue that the character chose well, or that the story itself is making a case for one loyalty over another. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Growing Up and the Loss of Innocence
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about growing up. Using a text we’ve read, explore how a character changes as they lose some illusion about the world, other people, or themselves — and what they gain or lose in the process.

You might trace a single turning point, or follow a character across the whole story. Consider whether the text treats growing up as a gift, a wound, or something more complicated. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Power and the People Who Hold It
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about power. Using a text we’ve read, examine how power is won, used, or lost — and what it reveals about the people who hold it.

You might focus on a character who gains power and is changed by it, on the people that power is used against, or on the way the text itself seems to define power. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Romeo and Juliet
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on Romeo and Juliet. You can choose any aspect of the play that interests you. Consider the themes we’ve discussed, the characters, the settings, or anything you’ve noticed about the story that you think is worthy of discussion.

In figuring out what to write about, consider your favorite character or favorite scene. What about this play entertained you or upset you? Maybe you liked the language of the play and how that affected your experience as a reader. Maybe a particular theme resonated with you. Maybe there’s a specific, favorite character you want to discuss. If you go to your emotional charge — what you loved, what grabbed your attention — you’ll find your topic.

Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the play to support your ideas. Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: A Character Who Stayed With You
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about a character from a text we’ve read who stayed with you. Choose someone you found yourself thinking about after you closed the book — someone you admired, distrusted, pitied, or couldn’t quite figure out.

Make an argument about who this character really is, what drives them, or how they change. Don’t just describe them; take a position other readers might disagree with. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

title: The Moment Everything Turns
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about the turning point in a text we’ve read. Identify the single moment where the story — or a character — changes course, and argue for why that moment matters more than any other.

Consider what is different before and after, and what the author does to make the moment land. You might even argue that the real turning point isn’t the obvious one. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Argue With the Author
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay that argues with the author of a text we’ve read. Identify a claim the text seems to make — about people, society, right and wrong, or the way the world works — and take a position on whether the author gets it right.

You might agree and push the idea further, disagree and explain where the text goes wrong, or complicate the claim by showing where it holds and where it breaks down. Be fair to the text before you challenge it. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: What History Means to You
prompt:
Using a specific historical figure, era, movement, or event, write an essay about what history means to you. Use your existing knowledge of history, as well as your personal experience and observations, to develop your position.

You might consider how the specific person, event, or movement aligns with your beliefs or worldview, or how they have shaped your opinions. You might also consider what they teach you about the world, our country, or people in general. If you’re having trouble choosing, go where the emotional charge is: start with what you find interesting, fascinating, or upsetting; choose a historical figure that you really admire or despise.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, supporting evidence, and a conclusion.

Be fair to the text: use what’s actually on the page to show where the character’s motives are more understandable — or more disturbing — than they first appear. Don’t excuse them; explain them. title: Beloved
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on Beloved. You can choose any aspect of the novel that interests you — the themes we’ve discussed, Sethe and Denver, the house on Bluestone Road, or the way Morrison tells a story that keeps circling back on itself.

Maybe you want to argue about what Beloved herself represents, about how memory works in the novel, or about what it means for a community to help or fail someone. Begin with the passage you could not stop thinking about and let it lead you to your claim. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the novel to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: The House on Mango Street
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on The House on Mango Street. You can choose any aspect of the book that interests you — the themes we’ve discussed, Esperanza’s voice, the neighbors whose stories she tells, or the way the book is built out of short chapters instead of one long narrative.

Maybe you want to argue about what home means to Esperanza, about what she is trying to leave and what she promises to come back for, or about why a particular vignette matters far more than its length suggests. Start with the chapter that stayed with you and build from there. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the book to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Things Fall Apart
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on Things Fall Apart. You can choose any aspect of the novel that interests you — the themes we’ve discussed, Okonkwo and his fear of weakness, the world of Umuofia, or what changes when the missionaries arrive.

Maybe you want to argue about whether Okonkwo is a tragic hero or a man undone by his own rigidity, about what Achebe wants you to see in Igbo life before the colonizers, or about the meaning of the novel’s final page. Go where the emotional charge is — what moved you, what angered you — and start your argument there. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the novel to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Hamlet
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on Hamlet. You can choose any aspect of the play that interests you — the themes we’ve discussed, the characters, the soliloquies, or anything in the language you noticed and want to argue about.

Maybe you want to argue about why Hamlet delays, about whether his madness is performance or real, or about how Ophelia, Gertrude, or Laertes changes the way you read him. Begin with the speech or scene that grabbed you and follow it to your thesis. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the play to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Julius Caesar
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on Julius Caesar. You can choose any aspect of the play that interests you — the themes we’ve discussed, the conspirators, the crowd, or the speeches that turn Rome one way and then the other.

Maybe you want to argue about whether Brutus is honorable or self-deceiving, about how Antony wins the crowd with words alone, or about what the play says about power and the people who hand it over. Start with the character you would defend or prosecute and build your case. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the play to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: The Kite Runner
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on The Kite Runner. You can choose any aspect of the novel that interests you — the themes we’ve discussed, Amir and Hassan, fathers and sons, or the way the past keeps returning.

Maybe you want to argue about whether Amir earns his redemption, about what Baba’s secret changes, or about how guilt shapes the person Amir becomes. Go where the emotional charge is — the scene you could not shake — and let it lead you to your claim. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the novel to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Antigone
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on Antigone. You can choose any aspect of the play that interests you — the themes we’ve discussed, Antigone and Creon, the chorus, or the collision between the law of the city and the law of the family.

Maybe you want to argue about who is right, about whether Creon’s change of heart comes too late to matter, or about what the play says about stubbornness in people who believe they are good. Take the side you actually believe and make the strongest case for it. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the play to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: The Scarlet Letter
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on The Scarlet Letter. You can choose any aspect of the novel that interests you — the themes we’ve discussed, Hester and Dimmesdale, the townspeople, or the symbols Hawthorne keeps turning over.

Maybe you want to argue about what the letter comes to mean by the end, about who is punished most and by whom, or about how the community uses shame to hold itself together. Start with the character you find hardest to judge and work outward from there. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the novel to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Persepolis
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on Persepolis. You can choose any aspect of the book that interests you — the themes we’ve discussed, Marji’s growing up, her family, or the choices Satrapi makes in the drawings themselves.

Maybe you want to argue about how the black-and-white images carry meaning the words do not, about what Marji learns to hide and what she refuses to, or about what the book shows you about a place you may only have seen in headlines. Begin with the panel or moment that struck you and build your argument from there. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations and images from the book to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: The Hate U Give
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on The Hate U Give. You can choose any aspect of the novel that interests you — the themes we’ve discussed, Starr’s two worlds, her family, or the way the novel handles a story we also see on the news.

Maybe you want to argue about what it costs Starr to speak, about how the book asks you to think about community and protest, or about why one character’s reaction complicates an easy reading of the novel. Go where the emotional charge is and start there. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the novel to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Identity and the Roles We’re Handed
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about identity — who a character is, who they are told to be, and the distance between the two. Drawing on a text we’ve read together, explore what the story suggests about becoming yourself in a world that keeps handing you a role.

You might focus on a character who is renamed, misread, or expected to be something they are not, or compare two characters who handle that pressure in opposite ways. Consider what the text treats as the truest version of a person. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Freedom and Its Limits
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about freedom and where it ends. Drawing on a text we’ve read together, explore how much freedom a character really has — and what stands in the way: law, family, money, fear, or something they carry inside them.

You might focus on a character who wants out of something, or on a moment when a choice turns out to be far less free than it looked. Consider whether the text treats freedom as something granted, taken, or earned. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Grief and What Comes After
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about grief and what people do with it. Drawing on a text we’ve read together, explore what the story suggests about loss — how characters carry it, avoid it, or are remade by it.

You might focus on a single character in mourning, or compare two characters who lose the same thing and respond in opposite ways. Consider whether the text offers any kind of consolation, and whether you believe it. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Money, Class, and Who Gets Ahead
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about money and class. Drawing on a text we’ve read together, explore what the story suggests about who gets ahead, who does not, and how much of that is settled before the characters ever make a choice.

You might focus on a character whose options are shaped by what they have or lack, or compare how two characters on different rungs see the same event. Consider whether the text believes moving up is actually possible. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Memory and the Stories We Tell
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about memory. Drawing on a text we’ve read together, explore what the story suggests about the past — how characters remember it, revise it, or are held by it.

You might focus on a character whose account of events you do not entirely trust, on a memory the text returns to again and again, or on the gap between what happened and what gets told. Consider what the text says about why people remember the way they do. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Courage in Small Moments
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about courage. Drawing on a text we’ve read together, explore what the story treats as brave — and whether the bravest thing in it is also the loudest.

You might focus on a quiet act that costs a character more than an obviously heroic one, or compare a character everyone calls brave with one nobody notices. Consider what the text seems to believe courage is for. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Family and What We Inherit
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about inheritance — not money, but everything else a family passes down: expectations, silences, tempers, loyalties, wounds. Drawing on a text we’ve read together, explore what the story suggests about what characters receive from the people who raised them.

You might focus on a parent and a child who make the same mistake, or on a character working hard not to become someone. Consider whether the text believes anyone fully escapes what they were given. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: People and the Natural World
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about the natural world in a text we’ve read together. Explore what the story suggests about the relationship between people and the land, the weather, the sea, or the animals around them — indifferent, hostile, healing, or something else entirely.

You might focus on a landscape that shapes the characters’ lives, on a storm or a season that arrives at exactly the wrong moment, or on a character who is at home outdoors in a way they never are among people. Consider what the text gains by putting nature where it does. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Truth, Lies, and the Stories Characters Tell
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about lying. Drawing on a text we’ve read together, explore what the story suggests about the lies characters tell each other — and the ones they tell themselves.

You might focus on a single deception and everything it sets in motion, or on a character whose self-deception does more damage than any lie told to them. Consider whether the text ever treats a lie as the right choice. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Revenge and What It Costs
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about revenge. Drawing on a text we’ve read together, explore what the story suggests about the desire to get even — where it comes from, what it promises, and what it actually delivers.

You might focus on a character whose need for revenge organizes their whole life, or compare someone who takes it with someone who lets it go. Consider whether the text treats revenge as justice, as poison, or as both at once. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: The Narrator You Can’t Quite Trust
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about how a text we’ve read is told. Argue that the narrator shapes what you believe — that this would be a different story in someone else’s hands.

Show where the telling tilts: what the narrator emphasizes, skips, excuses, or gets wrong. Make a claim about what that narration does to your judgment of the characters. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: A Minor Character Who Matters
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about a minor character in a text we’ve read. Argue that this character — someone easy to skim past — is doing more work in the story than their few pages suggest.

Show what the story would lose without them: what they reveal about the main characters, what they make possible, or what they quietly stand for. Make a case, not a summary. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: The First Page and the Last
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about the opening and the ending of a text we’ve read. Argue for what the distance between them means — what has changed by the last page, and what stubbornly has not.

Read both closely: the images, the tone, the words the author chose to start and to finish with. Make a claim about what the ending asks you to understand about the beginning. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: What the Author Left Out
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about a silence in a text we’ve read — a scene we never get, a character who never explains themselves, a question the book refuses to answer.

Argue for why the gap is there and what it does to you as a reader. Be specific: build your case from what is on the page around the absence. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Two Texts in Conversation
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay that puts two texts we’ve read into conversation. Argue for something neither one shows you alone — an agreement, a disagreement, or a question they answer in different ways.

Choose the pairing that genuinely interests you, and make sure the essay is an argument rather than a list of similarities and differences. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from both texts to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: A Line You Can’t Forget
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay built out of a single line from a text we’ve read — the sentence you underlined, quoted to someone, or still hear in your head.

Argue for why that line carries the weight it does, and what it opens up in the rest of the work. Stay close to the words themselves before you widen out. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: The Adaptation and the Original
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay comparing a text we’ve read with a film, play, or other adaptation of it. Argue for what the adaptation understands about the original — and what it loses, changes, or gets wrong.

Focus on specific choices: a cut scene, a recast character, a rewritten ending, a mood built out of images instead of sentences. Make an argument about meaning, not a list of differences. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text and details from the adaptation to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Who Gets to Speak
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about voice and power in a text we’ve read. Argue for what the book does with the question of who gets to speak, who is spoken about, and who is never heard from at all.

Show it in the text’s own structure: whose thoughts you have access to, whose dialogue is quoted, whose story arrives secondhand. Make a claim about what that arrangement means. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: The Text and Its Time
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about a text we’ve read and the world it came out of. Argue for how the time and place of its writing shows up in the work — in what it worries about, what it takes for granted, or what it dares to say.

Be specific about the connection rather than gesturing at history in general, and be honest about where the text still speaks to now and where it does not. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the text to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, supporting evidence, and a conclusion.

title: A Primary Source Worth Reading Closely
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about a single primary source — a letter, a diary entry, a photograph, a speech, a law, an advertisement — from the period we’ve been studying. Argue for what it reveals about the people who made it and the world they lived in.

Read it closely before you widen out: who wrote it, for whom, and what they assumed their reader already believed. Notice what it says without meaning to. Use your knowledge of the period and your own observations to develop your position, and evidence from the source to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, supporting evidence, and a conclusion.

title: A Movement and Its Legacy
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about a social or political movement and what it actually changed. Choose a movement you find compelling and argue for how we should measure what it accomplished.

Be honest about the ledger: what shifted, what did not, and what came later that the people involved never intended. If you are having trouble choosing, go where the emotional charge is — start with a movement you admire, or one you think is badly remembered. Use your knowledge of history and your own observations to develop your position, and evidence to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, supporting evidence, and a conclusion.

title: Two Accounts of the Same Event
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about two accounts of the same historical event that do not agree. Argue for what the disagreement itself reveals — about the sources, about the people who made them, or about the event.

Do not simply pick a winner. Look at who was writing, when, for whom, and with what at stake, and make a claim about how the two should be read together. Use your knowledge of the period and your own analysis to develop your position, and evidence from both accounts to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, supporting evidence, and a conclusion.

title: A Local History Nobody Teaches
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about a piece of history from where you live that never makes it into the textbook — a building, a street name, a factory, a school, a protest, a family that shaped the place.

Argue for why it deserves to be known, and be specific about what it explains about your town or city today. Talk to people, look at what has been written down, and be careful about what you can and cannot claim. Use your research, personal experience, and observations to develop your position, and evidence to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, supporting evidence, and a conclusion.

title: The Ethics of a New Technology
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about a scientific or technological development and whether we are ready for it. Choose something real — gene editing, artificial intelligence, self-driving cars, data collection, geoengineering — and argue for how it should be used or limited.

Explain the science accurately enough that your reader can follow you, then make an actual claim about what we owe one another in how we use it. Take the strongest objection seriously rather than the easiest one. Use your knowledge and observations to develop your position, and evidence to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, supporting evidence, and a conclusion.

title: An Idea People Refused to Believe
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about a scientific idea that people resisted before they accepted it. Choose one that interests you — the shape of the solar system, germ theory, evolution, plate tectonics, vaccination — and argue for what the resistance was really about.

Look past “people were wrong”: what did the idea cost them to believe, and who had a reason to fight it? Consider what the episode suggests about how we decide what is true now. Use your knowledge and observations to develop your position, and evidence to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, supporting evidence, and a conclusion.

title: A Chart That Misleads
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about a chart, graph, or map that tells its story badly. Find a real one — in the news, in an ad, in a report, on social media — and argue for what it hides, exaggerates, or invites you to conclude.

Be precise: what is on each axis, what has been left off, and what the design does to your eye before you have read a single number. Then argue for what an honest version would show. Use the data and your own analysis to develop and support your position.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, supporting evidence, and a conclusion.

title: A Song That Says Something
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay about a song or an album that does more than sound good. Argue for what it is saying — about a moment, a place, a feeling, or the person who made it.

Treat the lyrics like a text and the music like part of the argument: what the words claim, and what the sound does to them. Choose something you love, or something you cannot stop arguing about. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and quotations from the lyrics and details from the music to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: A Film Worth Arguing About
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven critical essay on a film. Choose one that is genuinely worth arguing about — great, overrated, misunderstood, or stranger than people admit — and make a claim about what it is doing.

Build your case out of specific choices: a shot, a cut, a performance, a line of dialogue, the way the ending lands. Go where the emotional charge is: what thrilled you, what bothered you, what you argued about afterward. Use your observations and opinions to develop your position, and details from the film to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: The Best Advice You’ve Been Given
prompt:
Write an essay about a piece of advice you were given and what you make of it now. It might be something that turned out to be true, something you followed for years before you questioned it, or something you were told that you think is flat-out wrong.

Argue for what you believe now, and be honest about how you got there. Use your personal experience and observations to develop your position, and evidence from your own life to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: A Place That Shaped You
prompt:
Write an essay about a place that shaped you — a house, a block, a field, a gym, a store, a single room. Argue for what that place did to the person you became.

Make a claim rather than a description: what the place taught you, gave you, or took from you. Go where the emotional charge is — the place you miss, or the one you were glad to leave. Use your personal experience and observations to develop your position, and evidence from your own life to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: What School Should Prepare You For
prompt:
Write a critical essay about what school should be preparing you for. Argue for what matters most — a job, college, citizenship, curiosity, becoming a decent person — and for what school does instead.

Be concrete about the gap you see, and propose what you would change. Use your personal experience and observations to develop your position, and evidence from your own life to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: The Case for an Unpopular Opinion
prompt:
Write a thesis-driven essay defending a position most people around you disagree with. Choose something you actually believe, not something you can argue for as an exercise.

Make the strongest version of the case, and take the best objection seriously instead of the weakest one. Persuasion is the point: write for a reader who starts out unconvinced. Use your observations and reasoning to develop your position, and evidence to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: Growing Up Online
prompt:
Write an essay about what it is like to grow up with the internet always on. Argue for what it has given your generation and what it has cost — attention, privacy, friendship, sleep, the ability to be bored.

Resist both easy stories: it is not all ruin, and it is not all connection. Use your personal experience and observations to develop your position, and evidence from your own life to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: What Fairness Actually Means
prompt:
Write an essay about fairness. Argue for what it actually means — treating everyone the same, giving people what they need, or something else — and test your definition against a real situation you have seen.

Choose the case that bothers you: a rule at school, a policy in your town, a decision in your family. Use your personal experience and observations to develop your position, and evidence from your own life to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: A Risk Worth Taking
prompt:
Write an essay about risk — one you took, one you did not, or one you are weighing right now. Argue for how a person should decide when a risk is worth it.

Be specific about the stakes and honest about the outcome, including if it went badly. Make a claim about what you learned that someone else could actually use. Use your personal experience and observations to develop your position, and evidence from your own life to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.

title: The Person Who Changed Your Mind
prompt:
Write an essay about a person who changed your mind about something. It might be a friend, a teacher, a relative, a stranger, or someone you have never met whose work reached you anyway.

Argue for how the change actually happened — what they said or did, why it landed, and what it took for you to let it. Use your personal experience and observations to develop your position, and evidence from your own life to support your ideas.

Your essay should be organized formally, with an introduction, thesis statement, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.
